veracity.statement: The household labour force survey showed that the unemployment rate increased from 4.6 to 4.8 percent in the quarter, and the quarterly employment survey showed that average hourly earnings increased 3.9 percent over the previous year.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two specific figures from the Stats NZ September 2024 quarter labour market release: an unemployment rate moving from 4.6% to 4.8%, and average hourly earnings up 3.9% year-on-year.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ labour market statistics for the September 2024 quarter: true if the HLFS unemployment rate is reported as rising from 4.6% to 4.8% and the QES average hourly earnings annual increase is 3.9%; false if either figure differs materially.

veracity.statement: The increase from 4.6 percent to 4.8 percent was lower than forecasters had been predicting. In its August Monetary Policy Statement, the Reserve Bank had forecast 5 percent unemployment and the Treasury had forecast 5.2 percent in the Budget update in May.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the outturn undershot official forecasts, and attributes two specific numbers to two named documents: the RBNZ August 2024 Monetary Policy Statement (5%) and the Treasury Budget Economic and Fiscal Update of May 2024 (5.2%).
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The RBNZ August 2024 Monetary Policy Statement forecast table and the Treasury May 2024 BEFU forecast table: true if they show unemployment forecasts of approximately 5.0% and 5.2% respectively for the period referenced, false if either figure is materially different or not attributable to those documents.

veracity.statement: To give some historical context, I would also point out to members that over the last 15 years, the average unemployment rate in New Zealand has been 5 percent.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific fifteen-year average for the New Zealand unemployment rate.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ HLFS quarterly unemployment rate series, mean of the quarters from late 2009 to late 2024: true if the mean is approximately 5.0% (within rounding), false if materially different.

veracity.statement: In the last year, wage growth has outpaced the cost of living in the first year of our new Government—compare that to the 13 quarters in a row under Labour, where wages grew slower than inflation.
veracity.explanation: Two factual assertions: that wage growth exceeded consumer price inflation over the year to the September 2024 quarter, and that there were thirteen consecutive quarters under the previous Labour government in which wage growth was below inflation.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ wage growth series (Labour Cost Index and/or QES average hourly earnings) against the CPI annual rate: true if the annual wage measure exceeds CPI for the year to the September 2024 quarter, and if there are 13 consecutive quarters during the 2017-2023 Labour government where the wage measure was below CPI; false if the recent year shows wages below CPI, or if the longest such run under Labour is not 13 quarters on a consistent measure.

veracity.statement: I haven’t seen that advice, but what I would say is that the Treaty is not changing and Treaty settlements are not changing.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Treaty Principles Bill leaves both the Treaty of Waitangi itself and concluded Treaty settlements untouched.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the Treaty Principles Bill as introduced, plus its regulatory impact statement and departmental advice: true if the bill contains no provision amending the text of the Treaty of Waitangi or the Treaty of Waitangi Act schedules, and no provision altering or reopening any concluded settlement Act or deed; false if it amends either.

specificity.statement: The household labour force survey showed that the unemployment rate increased from 4.6 to 4.8 percent in the quarter, and the quarterly employment survey showed that average hourly earnings increased 3.9 percent over the previous year.
specificity.explanation: Two named surveys, two exact rates and a stated reference period — fully checkable and actionable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The increase from 4.6 percent to 4.8 percent was lower than forecasters had been predicting. In its August Monetary Policy Statement, the Reserve Bank had forecast 5 percent unemployment and the Treasury had forecast 5.2 percent in the Budget update in May.

specificity.statement: Why does the Government believe that the principle of active protection, which places upon the Crown a positive duty to protect Māori interests and taonga, should be extinguished by an Act of Parliament?
specificity.explanation: Names a particular legal principle (active protection), states its content (a positive Crown duty over Māori interests and taonga) and identifies the mechanism at issue (extinguishment by statute). A precise question, checkable against the bill's text — though it stops short of citing the clause.

rigor.statement: Unemployment is rising and has been rising since 2001 because New Zealand has been in a prolonged recession, with monetary tightening used to drive high inflation out of the economy.
rigor.explanation: A causal argument is actually offered: recession plus deliberate monetary tightening to suppress inflation, leading to rising unemployment. The mechanism is a standard and coherent one, and the conclusion tracks the premises; no fallacy or appeal. Whether the stated start date is right is a Veracity matter and does not affect the inference.
rigor.subject: speaker

divination.statement: Now, there are clear indications that the economy has turned upwards, but even so, I would expect the unemployment rate to rise a bit further before beginning to fall.
divination.explanation: Forecasts the path of the unemployment rate: a further rise from 4.8%, followed by a turning point and decline. Not a promise about her own action.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ HLFS quarterly unemployment rate series after the September 2024 quarter: true if the rate rises above 4.8% and then records a sustained decline from its peak before the resolve-by date; false if it falls immediately without rising, or if it is still rising with no peak reached by that date.

focus.statement: Does he stand by his statement, “The Government has no plan, and never has had plans, to amend or revise the Treaty, or the Treaty settlements we have all worked so very hard together to achieve.”; if so, how does he reconcile that with the introduction tomorrow of a Government bill that completely rewrites the understanding of the Treaty upon which those settlements have been based?

civility.statement: Does he stand by his statement, “The Government has no plan, and never has had plans, to amend or revise the Treaty, or the Treaty settlements we have all worked so very hard together to achieve.”; if so, how does he reconcile that with the introduction tomorrow of a Government bill that completely rewrites the understanding of the Treaty upon which those settlements have been based?

veracity.statement: Yes, and in particular I stand by this Government’s action to conclude negotiations on a trade agreement with the Gulf Cooperation Council which will deliver duty-free access for 99 percent of New Zealand’s exports over 10 years.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that negotiations on an NZ–Gulf Cooperation Council trade agreement have been concluded, and that the agreement provides duty-free access for 99 percent of New Zealand's exports phased over 10 years.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MFAT's published NZ–GCC free trade agreement text and accompanying national interest analysis: true if negotiations were concluded before 5 November 2024 and the agreement provides for tariff elimination on ~99% of New Zealand's exports by value within 10 years; false if the tariff-elimination share or phase-in period is materially different, or if negotiations had not concluded.

veracity.statement: We operate very differently from the previous administration. We don’t need 16 reminders from the Cabinet Office to manage conflicts.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as fact that the previous (Labour) government received 16 reminders from the Cabinet Office about managing conflicts of interest. He asserts this himself rather than relaying it, so the claim is his own.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Cabinet Office correspondence released under the Official Information Act covering the 2017–2023 government: true if the Cabinet Office issued approximately 16 reminders to Ministers about conflict-of-interest management over that period, false if the count is materially different or no such reminders are recorded.

veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The New Zealand Health Survey daily smoking prevalence for adults, most recent release before 5 November 2024, and the Smokefree Aotearoa 2025 Action Plan target: true if the published daily smoking rate is 6.8% and the stated goal is under 5%, false if either figure is materially different.

veracity.statement: The survey also measures overall business confidence—a net 66 percent of businesses think that general business conditions will be better in 12 months’ time.

veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The ANZ Business Outlook survey release for October 2024: true if the headline business confidence net balance is approximately +66, false if materially different or if the figure quoted belongs to a different series (e.g. own-activity outlook).

veracity.statement: Inflation is back within the target band, and the Reserve Bank has begun reducing interest rates.

veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ CPI for the September 2024 quarter and the RBNZ Official Cash Rate decision record for 2024: true if annual CPI is between 1% and 3% and the OCR was lowered at one or more reviews before 5 November 2024, false if inflation is outside the band or no cut had occurred.

veracity.statement: Acknowledging the successful outcome for President Trump in the USA, does the Minister see any risk to Kiwi workers and our economy from the prospect of substantial tariffs in addition to those the last Trump administration imposed on New Zealand’s steel and aluminium exports; or from being, to use the Prime Minister’s words, a “force multiplier” for the USA under pillar 2 of AUKUS, which aims to contain China, our largest trading partner, which doesn’t impose tariffs on New Zealand exporters; or from the increasing global temperatures, droughts, and storm damage which will result if the USA withdraws from climate action?
veracity.explanation: Two checkable factual premises: that the first Trump administration imposed tariffs on New Zealand steel and aluminium exports, and that the Prime Minister used the phrase "force multiplier" about New Zealand's role under AUKUS pillar 2.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: US Section 232 proclamations of March 2018 and MFAT/NZ trade records on whether New Zealand steel and aluminium were subject to those tariffs; plus a documented quotation of Christopher Luxon using "force multiplier" in relation to AUKUS pillar 2. True if both are on the record, false if either is not.

veracity.statement: As that member will know, we’re about to re-engage with an administration where we got right on the cusp of a free-trade agreement; where he turned in front of the then Prime Minister—because of the work we’d done—and said to his team, “Well, why not?” We missed a chance then; we don’t intend to miss that chance this time.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that New Zealand came close to a free-trade agreement with the United States during the first Trump administration, and that Trump said "Well, why not?" to his team in front of the then Prime Minister.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: USTR and MFAT records on whether US–NZ FTA negotiations were formally launched or scoped in 2017–2020, and contemporaneous reporting or readouts of the Trump–Ardern meetings. True if an FTA process reached a formal or near-formal stage and the reported remark is documented; false if no negotiation process existed beyond general expressions of interest.

veracity.statement: The reality is that AUKUS is a work in progress with respect to pillar 2, and that member’s party was part and parcel of that arrangement—begun with a commissioned paper in September of 2021 under the then Labour Government; a report in October 2021—on which we have worked in the same way ever since, with no changes at all; so much so that the former defence Minister Andrew Little says that we have got it about right.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific documentary history: a paper commissioned in September 2021 and a report in October 2021 under the Labour Government, continuity of policy since with no changes, and that Andrew Little has said the current settings are about right.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MFAT/Defence official information releases dated September–October 2021 on AUKUS pillar 2, and a documented public statement by Andrew Little assessing the current government's AUKUS position. True if the dated documents exist and Little's statement is on the record, false if either is absent or materially mischaracterised.

veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Treasury proactive release pages for Project iReX. True if the iReX advice documents are published there and a December 2023 Cabinet decision declining further KiwiRail funding is recorded; false if no such release exists or the decision date differs.

veracity.falsification_criterion: Cabinet minutes and ministerial announcements on Cook Strait ferry replacement up to 7 November 2024. True if no decision on vessel type or freight arrangements had been taken by that date, false if one had.

veracity.falsification_criterion: Published interviews or statements by Don Braid in 2024 on the ferry replacement. specificity.statement: Does he agree with the Minister for Children that allowing providers to use force against children may be seen as “increasing the potential risk of abuse in custody”, and, if so, why is he allowing boot camp providers to use force on children, especially when it perpetuates the abuse in State care detailed in the Whanaketia report?

veracity.statement: Yes, and in particular I stand by this Government’s action to conclude negotiations on a trade agreement with the Gulf Cooperation Council which will deliver duty-free access for 99 percent of New Zealand’s exports over 10 years.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that negotiations on an FTA with the Gulf Cooperation Council have been concluded and that the deal delivers duty-free access for 99 percent of NZ exports phased over 10 years.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MFAT's published NZ–GCC FTA outcome documents and the negotiation-conclusion announcement: true if negotiations were concluded before 5 November 2024 and the published tariff outcomes show ~99% of NZ export value becoming duty-free within 10 years; false if negotiations were not concluded or the published coverage figure is materially lower.

veracity.statement: We’re down at 6.8 percent, heading to 5 percent to deliver on Smokefree Aotearoa 2025.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the daily smoking rate is currently 6.8 percent and that the Smokefree target is a 5 percent rate.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Health Survey daily smoking prevalence for the most recent year published before 5 November 2024, and the Smokefree Aotearoa 2025 Action Plan's stated target: true if the published adult daily smoking rate is 6.8% and the target is under 5%, false if the published rate is materially different.

veracity.statement: We operate very differently from the previous administration. We don’t need 16 reminders from the Cabinet Office to manage conflicts.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the previous (Labour) Government received 16 reminders from the Cabinet Office about managing conflicts of interest, and that the current Government has not needed such reminders.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Cabinet Office correspondence released under the OIA covering the 2017–2023 Government: true if the record shows approximately 16 reminders to Ministers about conflict-of-interest obligations, false if the number is materially different or no such reminders are documented.

veracity.statement: The survey also measures overall business confidence—a net 66 percent of businesses think that general business conditions will be better in 12 months’ time.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the ANZ Business Outlook survey most recently released before 5 November 2024 recorded net business confidence of 66 percent for conditions 12 months ahead.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The ANZ Business Outlook release for October 2024: true if headline net business confidence is approximately 66 (±1 rounding), false if materially different.

veracity.statement: Inflation is back within the target band, and the Reserve Bank has begun reducing interest rates.
veracity.explanation: Two present-tense claims: that annual CPI inflation is inside the RBNZ's 1–3 percent target band, and that the Reserve Bank has started cutting the OCR.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ CPI for the September 2024 quarter and the RBNZ Official Cash Rate decision record: true if annual CPI is between 1 and 3 percent and at least one OCR cut occurred before 5 November 2024, false if inflation is outside the band or no cut had been made.

veracity.statement: These are our most serious offenders, who must have committed at least two serious crimes with convictions of at least 10 years or more, which could be a range of things including sexual violence, aggravated robbery, or injury with intent to cause grievous bodily harm.

veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The publicly released Cabinet paper and the eligibility criteria in the resulting Oranga Tamariki (Responding to Serious Youth Offending) legislation: true if the criteria require two or more qualifying offences with a 10-year-plus maximum penalty, false if the threshold is lower or defined differently.

focus.statement: We operate very differently from the previous administration. We don’t need 16 reminders from the Cabinet Office to manage conflicts.
focus.explanation: There is a concrete accountability point here — a countable number of Cabinet Office reminders — but it is delivered as a general 'we are better than them' comparison rather than as engagement with the conflict-of-interest question asked.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.explanation: Entirely on the policy — the use-of-force power, the risk assessment attached to it, and the evidence base in the Whanaketia report. Scrutiny of a named measure, not party attack.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Will she, in this House, promise that for-profit organisations will never run these military-style academies?
focus.explanation: Squarely about a design feature of a named programme — who is permitted to operate it — with no party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Because I know that that Minister is determined to lower smoking rates across this country and is doing so incredibly passionately and is determined to do it.
rigor.explanation: Non sequitur: the question was how he can be confident conflicts of interest are being managed when he does not know who is advising the Minister. A Minister's determination and passion about an outcome is no evidence at all about conflict management — the conclusion does not follow from the premise offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Typically, unemployment lags economic activity, meaning that the unemployment rate will rise for a time, even as the economy picks up.
rigor.explanation: A stated general premise (unemployment is a lagging indicator) supports the specific conclusion drawn (the rate can keep rising during a recovery). The inference is valid on its own terms; whether the premise holds is a separate question.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I would have thought that the member on the other side would have wanted to create any ability for iwi and hapū to have some involvement in self-determination for what happens to their young people.
rigor.explanation: Strawman plus false dichotomy: the question was whether for-profit organisations would be barred from running the academies, and the answer recasts that as opposition to iwi and hapū involvement, as though ruling out for-profit providers necessarily rules out iwi providers. Nothing offered connects the two.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I’d just say to that member: if he cares a lot about conflicts, I wouldn’t call a sister-in-law a distant relative.
civility.explanation: Turns from the policy question to a personal jibe about the questioner's own family relationship, imputing hypocrisy and dishonesty to him personally rather than engaging the substance. He subsequently withdrew and apologised.
civility.subject: speaker

divination.statement: That will not continue for ever, however, and unemployment is expected to come down next year.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the unemployment rate will fall during 2025, after an expected period of further rises.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ Household Labour Force Survey unemployment rate through the four quarters of 2025: true if the rate peaks and then falls measurably within 2025, false if it is still flat or rising at the December 2025 quarter.

veracity.statement: The household labour force survey showed that the unemployment rate increased from 4.6 to 4.8 percent in the quarter, and the quarterly employment survey showed that average hourly earnings increased 3.9 percent over the previous year.

veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ Household Labour Force Survey, September 2024 quarter: true if the unemployment rate is 4.8%, revised up from 4.6% in the June quarter; false if materially different. Stats NZ Quarterly Employment Survey, September 2024 quarter: true if average hourly earnings rose 3.9% over the year, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: In its August Monetary Policy Statement, the Reserve Bank had forecast 5 percent unemployment and the Treasury had forecast 5.2 percent in the Budget update in May.
veracity.explanation: Asserts what two named institutions forecast for unemployment in two named documents: RBNZ August 2024 Monetary Policy Statement (5 percent) and Treasury's May 2024 Budget Economic and Fiscal Update (5.2 percent).
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The published forecast tables in the RBNZ Monetary Policy Statement of August 2024 and the Treasury Budget Economic and Fiscal Update of May 2024; true if the projected unemployment rate for the September 2024 quarter is 5.0% and 5.2% respectively, false if either differs materially.

veracity.statement: To give some historical context, I would also point out to members that over the last 15 years, the average unemployment rate in New Zealand has been 5 percent.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the mean New Zealand unemployment rate across the fifteen years to late 2024 is 5 percent.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Mean of the Stats NZ HLFS seasonally adjusted quarterly unemployment rate from Q4 2009 to Q3 2024; true if that mean rounds to 5.0%, false if it differs by more than a few tenths of a percentage point.

veracity.statement: In the last year, wage growth has outpaced the cost of living in the first year of our new Government—compare that to the 13 quarters in a row under Labour, where wages grew slower than inflation.

veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ annual wage growth (Labour Cost Index and/or QES average hourly earnings) against annual CPI inflation, quarter by quarter; true if the year to September 2024 shows wage growth above CPI and if a run of exactly 13 consecutive quarters of wage growth below CPI falls within the 2017-2023 Labour government, false if the run is shorter, longer, or does not exist on the standard series.

veracity.statement: Look, the only comment I'd add is that the bill hasn't been introduced to the Parliament.

specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Unemployment is rising and has been rising since 2001 because New Zealand has been in a prolonged recession, with monetary tightening used to drive high inflation out of the economy.
rigor.explanation: A complete causal chain is offered — monetary tightening to squeeze out inflation, which produces a recession, which raises unemployment — and the conclusion tracks the mechanism supplied. rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: As I have explained in this House before, it is Government policy to support this bill to first reading. The only way this bill will become law is if the Opposition parties do support it.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion follows from the premises supplied: if there is a free vote at second reading and the largest governing party will vote against, the bill cannot reach a majority without Opposition votes. No fallacy; the inference rests on stated seat arithmetic rather than on assertion.
rigor.subject: speaker

divination.statement: Now, there are clear indications that the economy has turned upwards, but even so, I would expect the unemployment rate to rise a bit further before beginning to fall.

divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ HLFS seasonally adjusted unemployment rate for quarters after September 2024; true if the rate rises above 4.8% in at least one subsequent quarter and then declines from that peak, false if it falls from 4.8% without a further rise or keeps rising with no decline by the resolve-by date.

veracity.statement: Will the Government consider moving an instruction to the committee to report the Treaty principles bill back to Parliament immediately, given there is no requirement in the coalition agreement for a full select committee process, and, if not, why not?

veracity.statement: Acknowledging the successful outcome for President Trump in the USA, does the Minister see any risk to Kiwi workers and our economy from the prospect of substantial tariffs in addition to those the last Trump administration imposed on New Zealand’s steel and aluminium exports; or from being, to use the Prime Minister’s words, a “force multiplier” for the USA under pillar 2 of AUKUS, which aims to contain China, our largest trading partner, which doesn’t impose tariffs on New Zealand exporters; or from the increasing global temperatures, droughts, and storm damage which will result if the USA withdraws from climate action?

veracity.statement: As that member will know, we’re about to re-engage with an administration where we got right on the cusp of a free-trade agreement; where he turned in front of the then Prime Minister—because of the work we’d done—and said to his team, “Well, why not?” We missed a chance then; we don’t intend to miss that chance this time.

veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: USTR and MFAT records of any US–NZ FTA negotiating mandate or launch during 2017–2020, plus contemporaneous readouts and reporting of the Trump–Ardern meetings; true if a negotiation was formally in prospect and the reported exchange is corroborated, false if no negotiating mandate existed and the exchange is uncorroborated.

veracity.statement: The reality is that AUKUS is a work in progress with respect to pillar 2, and that member’s party was part and parcel of that arrangement—begun with a commissioned paper in September of 2021 under the then Labour Government; a report in October 2021—on which we have worked in the same way ever since, with no changes at all; so much so that the former defence Minister Andrew Little says that we have got it about right.

veracity.statement: The question reflects some misunderstanding on the part of the member.
